title: God our mother
hook: Julian of Norwich wrote of Jesus as our true mother

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ockham's razor. Your line was keep it simple. Which extra part of a story did you cut? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

A woman lies so sick that the people around her expect her to die. A priest comes and holds a crucifix before her face. And then, as she later wrote, she was given a series of showings: visions of Christ and his love. She recovered. She went on thinking about what she had seen, and she wrote it down. We know her as Julian of Norwich, a woman who lived a life of prayer beside a church in that English city. Among the things she wrote is this: Jesus is our mother.

Julian wasn't throwing out the old words. She calls God our Father, plainly and often. But she sets the two side by side: as truly as God is our Father, God is our Mother. And she gives the motherhood above all to Jesus. Why Jesus? Look at what a mother does. She carries a child in her own body and brings it into life through pain. Julian looks at the cross and sees that: Christ laboring to bring us to birth. A mother feeds her child from herself. Julian sees Christ feeding his people with himself in the sacrament. A mother doesn't stop loving a child who falls in the mud; she picks it up and washes it. Julian says Christ does the same when we fail, without contempt. She didn't invent the picture out of nothing. Scripture already holds it. In Isaiah, God says, "As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you." And earlier: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee." Jesus himself, grieving over Jerusalem, says, "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings." Julian wove a picture like this into a whole way of seeing. Christians today use her picture in different ways. Some pray with her words. Others keep to the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer while still honoring her. Julian herself held both, and saw no contest between them.

Here's the practice: picture God's care as a mother's. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one picture of that kind of care, from your own life or one you've seen. A cool hand on a feverish forehead. A child lifted up after a fall. Someone awake in the middle of the night with a crying baby. If your own story with a mother is hard, choose a different picture; anyone who has cared like that will do. Let the picture stay a while. Then, if you pray, you can hold it up to God the way Julian did, and rest there. The bell holds the time.
God our mother. Julian of Norwich's picture of Christ who births, feeds and lifts us up, as truly as God is our Father.
Your line: our true mother. Today, care for one person the way a good mother would: quietly, practically, and without keeping score. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray with Julian of Norwich's words and read her Revelations of Divine Love; churches keep the Father language of the creeds and the Lord's Prayer, and some also use scripture's mother images for God's care, as in Isaiah 66:13.

fork.setup: you're Julian. on your sickbed you've seen Christ's love, and now you're searching for words for it. which picture do you reach for?
options: a judge reading out a sentence.
a mother who births, feeds, and picks up her child.
a king far away on a throne.
fork.reveal: Julian calls Jesus our true mother: laboring on the cross, feeding his people, lifting them when they fall. and she still calls God Father.

original.note: Hebrew, mother. In Isaiah 66:13 God's comfort is pictured as a mother's.

trapdoor: what you thought: calling God mother is a brand-new idea.
what it means: Julian saw Christ birthing, feeding and lifting us like a mother, while still calling God Father.
what a scholar hears: a picture scripture already holds, in Isaiah 49 and 66 and Matthew 23; Julian built it into a whole teaching.
recall: the Latin word for this love

sources.ref: Revelations of Divine Love, ch. 3 (the sickbed) and ch. 58–61 (Christ our mother)

notes: Julian is paraphrased throughout (no quotation of Warrack 1901); a scholar may want to add an exact Warrack line from ch. 59 or 60.
Sickbed details (expected to die, crucifix held before her face) follow ch. 2–3 of the Revelations; confirm chapter references.
'A woman who lived a life of prayer beside a church' describes her as an anchoress without details; confirm wording.
'Feeding his people with himself in the sacrament' paraphrases Julian ch. 60; confirm fair across churches.
Hebrew אֵם (mother) given as the general word; the form in Isaiah 66:13 is with a suffix (אִמּוֹ).
Editor pass: replaced 'still makes readers stop' (tells the listener a reaction); no longer claims Julian drew directly on the Isaiah and Matthew verses; pronunciation of אֵם corrected to 'EM'.
Audit (fresh reviewer): Isaiah 66:13, 49:15 and Matthew 23:37 checked against the KJV; Julian ch. 59–61 paraphrases fair; no change needed.
